## Ko wai te Pirimia o Aotearoa? | Who is the Prime Minister of New Zealand?

Ko **Christopher Luxon** te Pirimia o Aotearoa i tēnei wā — Christopher Luxon is the current prime minister of New Zealand, leading the National Party-led coalition government. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1)

The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government, with key responsibilities including appointing ministers, leading cabinet meetings, acting as spokesperson for the government, and providing advice to the governor-general — who represents King Charles III as head of state. [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1)

Luxon has consistently led the preferred prime minister polls, though his position has been contested by Labour leader Chris Hipkins in more recent polling. [[5]](cite://5/1)

## He aha ngā mahi a te Pirimia? | What does the Prime Minister do?

The role has evolved significantly over time. Since 1906, every leader of New Zealand has been formally sworn in as prime minister — a title reserved for self-governing dominions. [[6]](cite://6/1) From 1996, prime ministers have typically led coalition or minority governments under the Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) electoral system, requiring them to manage governments made up of several parties with differing values. [[3]](cite://3/2)

He pātai anō — would you like to know more about the history of New Zealand's prime ministers and how the role has changed over time?

His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? In the early 2000s there were four statues of former premiers and prime ministers in Wellington. Geographical features such as glaciers, mountains and rivers, and small towns, have also been named after leaders. 4.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's unique constitutional structure comprising multiple laws, court judgments, government documents, and conventions rather than a single written document. It covers foundational concepts including the landmark case Fitzgerald v Muldoon (1976), which established that the Prime Minister cannot suspend laws. The document details the executive, legislative, and independent judiciary structures with separation of powers. It examines New Zealand's constitutional evolution around two pillars: the Treaty of Waitangi (1840)—an agreement between the British Crown and Māori chiefs—and representative democracy, with voting rights extended to all adult males (1879) and women (1893). The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) reinterpreted the Treaty's meaning in the late 20th century. Mixed-member proportional representation (1996) fundamentally altered constitutional dynamics. The document traces executive power evolution from the 1930s-1990s, describing how reforms including the Official Information Act 1982 and Bill of Rights Act 1990 limited executive authority. New Zealand's constitution is notably flexible, changing through statute amendments and convention shifts, with citizens protected through complaint mechanisms including ombudsmen and human rights commissions. Parliament maintains supremacy stronger than other Westminster democracies.

8.text:
[Page 1] New Zealand’s system of government New Zealand is a parliamentary democracy. The prime minister is the head of New Zealand’s government, which must have the support of the majority of members of Parliament. The country’s laws are made by Parliament, which is based on the British Westminster system. New Zealanders aged 18 and over can vote for members of Parliament (MPs). Elections are held every three years. Under the mixed member proportional system (MMP), New Zealanders cast two votes one for a political party, and one for a local MP. The number of seats each party gains in Parliament is decided by how much of the total party vote the party gets. New Zealand is fully independent, but it is also a constitutional monarchy: the head of state is King Charles III. He is represented in New Zealand by the governor general, who traditionally does what the government advises him or her to do. The Treaty of Waitangi The Treaty of Waitangi is the founding document of modern New Zealand. It is named after the place in the Bay of Islands where it was first signed on 6 February 1840. It was signed by William Hobson and other people representing the British Crown (Queen Victoria), and a large number of Māori chiefs. The chiefs agreed that the British should have some authority in New Zealand, and that European people could settle there. They understood that in turn they would keep their own lands and customs, and that the authority of the chiefs would remain. Promises made to Māori in the treaty were not always kept, and there is debate about what it means. The Waitangi Tribunal deals with claims from Māori tribes about their land and other issues to do with the treaty. Independence and nationhood Thousands of settlers, mostly from England, Scotland and Ireland, began to arrive in New Zealand in the 1840s, and they set up their own government in the 1850s. Over the next 150 years the country became less dependent on the British government. But there are still many signs of the historic link with Britain for example, the monarch’s head appears on New Zealand coins. New Zealand is a small independent country which plays an active role in the United Nations and the Commonwealth. It is a distinctive nation, with its own traditions and ways of life. 9.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's rights and equality in New Zealand from the 19th century to the early 21st century across multiple domains. It examines how colonisation undermined Māori women's traditional power and how European settlers' gender ideologies shaped laws, property rights, education, and employment. 27.document_title: 'The prime minister is dying': 50 years since Norman Kirk's last public appearance
27.document_summary: This article commemorates the 50th anniversary of Norman Kirk's final public appearance on August 18, 1974, at St Peter's College in Palmerston North, New Zealand. Despite severe illness—including an enlarged heart, blood clot in his lungs, and liver problems—Kirk insisted on attending the school opening ceremony for his friend Joe Walding. His wife Ruth confided to the school's board chair that "the prime minister is dying." Kirk died 13 days later on August 31, 1974, aged 51, making him the first New Zealand prime minister to die in office since 1940. During his two-year tenure, Kirk's government recognized China, protested French nuclear testing, refused entry to a racially selected Springbok rugby team, and introduced a retirement savings scheme. The article features insights from his private secretary Margaret Hayward and reflects on how Kirk's death prompted massive public grief followed by rapid public amnesia as successor Bill Rowling took office.

3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

chunkHighlights.text:
The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among
those forming the government. His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor-general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self-government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self-government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? In the early 2000s there were four statues of former premiers and prime ministers in Wellington. Geographical features such as glaciers,
mountains and rivers, and small towns, have also been named after

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of New Zealand's political system, constitutional development, and national identity. It covers New Zealand's parliamentary democracy structure with a mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system where citizens aged 18+ vote for both political parties and local MPs every three years. The document details the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), the founding document between British representatives and Māori chiefs, which established British authority while promising Māori land rights and cultural preservation, though it notes significant translation discrepancies between English and Māori versions. New Zealand's evolution from a British colony to an independent nation is traced through the establishment of self-government in 1856, adoption of the Statute of Westminster in 1947, and the Constitution Act of 1986. The parliamentary structure comprises 120 seats (65 general, 7 Māori, 48 party list), with the cabinet as the most powerful political body. The document covers state sector governance including 38 departments/ministries, Crown entities, and state-owned enterprises. New Zealand's legal system hierarchy includes District Courts, High Court, Court of Appeal, and Supreme Court, with local government comprising 61 territorial councils and 11 regional councils. The Waitangi Tribunal, created in 1975, addresses Māori grievances. National identity elements include citizenship laws (1948), national symbols (kiwi bird, silver fern, pōhutukawa), and official languages (Māori since 1987, sign language since 2006). The document concludes with New Zealand's international relations, including ANZUS alliance with the United States, close ties with Australia, constitutional relationships with Pacific territories, and participation in the UN, Commonwealth, WTO, APEC, and CPTPP.

chunkHighlights.text:
New Zealand’s system of government New Zealand is a parliamentary
democracy. The prime minister is the head of New Zealand’s government, which must have the support of the majority of members of Parliament. The country’s laws are made by Parliament, which is based on the British Westminster system. New Zealanders aged 18 and over can vote for members of Parliament (MPs). Elections are held every three years. Under the mixed-member proportional system (MMP), New Zealanders cast two votes – one for a political party, and one for a local MP. The number of seats each party gains in Parliament is decided by how much of the total party vote the party gets. New Zealand is fully independent, but it is also a constitutional monarchy: the head of state is King Charles III. He is represented in New Zealand by the governor-general, who traditionally does what the government advises him or her to do. The Treaty of Waitangi The Treaty of Waitangi is the founding document of modern New Zealand. It is named after the place in the Bay of Islands where it was first signed on 6 February 1840. It was signed by William Hobson and other people representing the British Crown (Queen Victoria), and a large number of Māori chiefs. The chiefs agreed that the British should have some authority in New Zealand, and that European people could settle there. They understood that in turn they would keep their own lands and customs, and that the authority of the chiefs would remain. Promises made to Māori in the treaty were not always kept, and there is debate about what it means. The Waitangi Tribunal deals with claims from Māori tribes about their land and other issues to do with the treaty. Independence and nationhood Thousands of settlers, mostly from England, Scotland and Ireland, began to arrive in New Zealand in the 1840s, and they set up their own government in the 1850s. Over the next 150 years the country became less dependent on the British government. But there are still many signs of the historic link with Britain – for example, the monarch’s head appears on New Zealand coins. New Zealand is a small independent country which plays an active
role in the United Nations and the Commonwealth. It is a distinctive
nation, with its own traditions and ways of life. It has its own flag, coat of
arms, national anthem and national holidays.

5.fileDescription: According to the latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, Labour leads National by eight percentage points with 38% support compared to National's 30%. Labour leader Chris Hipkins is the preferred prime minister at 45%, ahead of Christopher Luxon at 39%. Labour's coalition partners (Greens at 8% and Te Pāti Māori at 2%) could potentially form a government with Labour, achieving a bare majority of 61 seats. National's coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First poll at 8% and 9% respectively. Neither the current coalition nor opposition has clear governing numbers.

Labour has an eight-point lead over National in the latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, but neither the coalition nor the opposition parties have the numbers to govern. Labour has 38 percent support in the poll, up four points since the last survey in October, compared to National on 30 percent, down one point. National's coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First are on 8 and 9 percent respectively. The Greens are registering 8 percent - down one - with Te Pāti Māori on two percent - also down one. On this result, Labour could potentially form a government with the support of the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, assuming Te Pāti Māori wins one electorate. They would have 61 seats between them - the barest majority. Labour leader Chris Hipkins is still the preferred prime minister on 45 percent, while Christopher Luxon is at 39 percent, although Luxon has gained 3 points since the last The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll in October. 6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

Premiers and prime ministers The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among
those forming the government. His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor-general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self-government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self-government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? There have been three women prime ministers: Jenny Shipley (1997 99), who led the National Party from 1997 to 2001; Helen Clark (1999 2008), the first woman to become prime minister following an election, who was leader of the Labour Party from 1993 to 2008; and Jacinda Ardern (2017 23}, who became leader of the Labour Party in August 2017 and prime minister less than three months later. [Page 7] Religion was politically divisive in the early 1900s when Sir Joseph Ward (a Catholic) and William Massey (Protestant) led the major parties, Liberal and Reform. Generally, though, it seldom raised political ripples in New Zealand. Because the Anglican Church is not an established (that is, official state) church in New Zealand, Frederick Weld, a Catholic, could become premier in 1864. Julius Vogel, who was Jewish, became premier in 1873. By contrast, in 2017 Britain had still not had a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Non belief was also not a bar to office in New Zealand; colonial premiers Alfred Domett, Robert Stout and John Ballance were freethinkers.

He holds a pipe in his mouth, a common practice among Māori people. The photograph bears the name stamp of photographer Alfred Burton, who acquired a collection of negatives from the original photographer, McGarrigle. McGarrigle’s Māori portraits often resemble contemporary photographs of Native Americans, though there is no evidence he visited the U.S. Photographers of that era commonly used a wardrobe of clothes and accessories for their subjects.
